extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament (Lords and Commons), lawmakers, learned men, and the reading public
extracted.subtask_description: A seventeenth‑century polemic (Milton's Areopagitica) opposing statutory licensing and censorship of books; it argues for freedom to print, publish, and read without pre‑publication approval. The page addresses the procedures, effects, and moral/political consequences of licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory pre‑reading of foreign books
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordain that no forrein books be deliver'd out of custody, till they have bin read over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural requirement would place all foreign books in custody until read by appointed officers; Milton criticizes this as onerous and ineffective, noting it would require many overseers and slow the importation of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue and forbid offending printers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the multitude of books encrease upon their hands, ye must be fain to catalogue all those Printers who are found frequently offending, and forbidd the importation of their whole suspected typography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order proposes listing repeat‑offending printers and banning their typefaces/works; Milton treats this as a punitive, monopolistic measure that would stifle trade and learning and is likely to be abused or misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expurgation/expunction of mixed books
rubrics_metrics.description: There be also books which are partly useful and excellent, partly culpable and pernicious; this work will ask as many more officials to make expurgations and expunctions, that the Commonwealth of learning be not damnify'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy expects officials to excise objectionable passages from works that are otherwise valuable. Milton argues this demands more officials and will mutilate important writings, risking loss of meaning and harm to posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model licensing on Trent and Seville
rubrics_metrics.description: Ye must reform it perfectly according to the model of Trent and Sevil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed reform is to imitate continental (Inquisition) censorship models; Milton warns that such conformity would import oppressive, servile restrictions and is to be abhorred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensers must be 'studious, learned, and judicious'
rubrics_metrics.description: He who is made judge to sit upon the birth or death of books ... had need to be a man above the common measure both studious, learned, and judicious; there may be else no mean mistakes in the censure of what is passable or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensing is to be defensible, Milton admits the licenser would require exceptional learning and judgement; he uses this to show the impracticality of the scheme and the rarity of suitable appointees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing imposes impractical perpetual reader duty
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a more tedious and unpleasing journey-work, a greater losse of time levied upon his head, then to be made the perpetuall reader of unchosen books and pamphlets, oftimes huge volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton emphasises the time, tedium, and moral cost of forcing learned men to read everything at all times; as a practical guideline this counsels against creating duties that require continuous, exhaustive review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selecting licensers by pecuniary or low motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing therefore those who now possesse the imployment ... wish themselves well ridd of it, and that no man of worth ... is ever likely to succeed them, except he mean to put himself to the salary of a Presse-corrector, we may easily foresee what kind of licencers we are to expect hereafter, either ignorant, imperious, and remisse, or basely pecuniary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton warns that the office will attract the unworthy (mercenary or incompetent), producing poor censorship; the implicit criterion is to avoid institutional designs that select for low‑quality officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect authorial dignity and autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: So far to distrust the judgement and the honesty of one who hath but a common repute in learning ... as not to count him fit to print his mind without a tutor and examiner, is the greatest displeasure and indignity to a free and knowing spirit that can be put upon him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement that authors submit to tutors/examiners before publishing is condemned as dishonouring and stifling; the guideline is to trust authors' responsibility and preserve their dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit authors to revise during printing
rubrics_metrics.description: What if the author shall be one so copious of fancy as to have many things well worth the adding come into his mind after Hcencing, while the book is yet under the Presse ... The Printer dares not go beyond his licenc't copy ; so often then must the author trudge to his leav- giver ... mean while either the Presse must stand still ... or the author loose his accuratest thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues licensing prevents normal creative processes (late additions/edits) and delays printing; a practical standard is to allow authors latitude to modify works during production without bureaucratic stoppage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing silences and mutilates posthumous works
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work of any deceased author ... come to their hands for licence to be Printed or Reprinted, if there be found in his book one sentence of a ventrous edge ... they will not pardon him their dash; the sense of that great man shall to all posterity be lost for the fearfulnesse or the presumptuous rashnesse of a perfunctory licencer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton warns that overcautious licensers will expunge historically important or bold statements from deceased authors, depriving posterity of insight; guideline: avoid censoring historical works out of timorousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not monopolize knowledge by tickets and statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and understanding are not such wares as to be monopoliz'd and traded in by tickets and statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton condemns treating knowledge as a commodity controlled by licences or statutory stamps; the normative standard is free circulation and open access to ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust the common people with books
rubrics_metrics.description: If we so jealous over them as that we dare not trust them with an English pamphlet, what doe we but censure them for a giddy, vitious, and ungrounded people ... That this is care or love of them, we cannot pretend, whenas in those Popish places where the Laity are most hated and despis'd the same strictnes is us'd over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues against paternalistic restrictions on lay readers; the guideline is to presume competence and avoid measures that patronize or degrade the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing breeds attraction to forbidden writings (counterproductive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A forbidd'n writing is thought to be a certain spark of truth ... This order therefore may prove a nursing mother to sects, but I shall easily shew how it will be a step-dame to Truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton suggests prohibition increases the allure and prestige of banned works and can nurture sectarianism; as an evaluative principle, suppression is counterproductive to social stability and truth‑finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and truth thrive by exercise and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Well knows he who uses to consider, that our faith and knowledge thrives by exercise as well as our limbs and coinplexron. Truth is compared in Scripture to a streaming fountain; if her waters flow not in a perpetuall progression, they sick'n into a muddy pool of conformity and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton asserts that continual publication, debate, correction, and testing keep knowledge healthy; the practical standard is to encourage open discourse and the free exchange of ideas so truth can be examined and advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow learned men to publish dissenting views openly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man judicious, learned, and of a conscience ... shall not privily from house to house ... but openly by writing publish to the world what his opinion is, what his reasons, and wherefore that which is now thought cannot be sound?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton emphasizes the importance of public, written refutation and debate by qualified persons as a check on received opinion; licensing that prevents such publication thwarts correction and progress.
